content:
alex: heads up — ran an nsys profile inside the standard staging container and the timeline is missing entire kernel groups. looks like a regression vs last week, but only inside k8s. anyone seen this?

sara: hmm, were you running under user namespaces / rootless pod? we've seen nsight timelines truncated when containers aren't privileged.

alex: yes rootless (no --privileged). run command was:
```
docker run --gpus all -v /tmp/traces:/traces --rm my-infer-image 
  nsys profile --output /traces/run1 --stats true --force-overwrite true -- 
  ./server --model foo
```
I get a tiny .qdrep and no cuda kernel timeline. nvprof also shows a handful of kernels only.

jordan: that matches a seccomp/userns/uidmap issue. nvidia-container-toolkit can require extra caps for in-kernel timestamps. try either --privileged or at least `--cap-add SYS_ADMIN --security-opt seccomp=unconfined`.

maria: fwiw we saw a related failure where trace files were created as root in /tmp and CI couldn't access them (permission denied) so the job looked like "no timeline". check ownership: `ls -l /tmp/traces`

alex: confirmed — the .qdrep is 0 bytes and owned by root:root even though the container ran as 1000:1000. not sure how it became root.

devbot: CI log snippet:
```
[2024-11-05 14:03:21] run-profile.sh: starting nsys
[2024-11-05 14:03:23] nsys: error: failed to write timeline file: Permission denied
[2024-11-05 14:03:23] run-profile.sh: exiting 1
```

sara: okay two separate issues then: (1) permission/ownership for trace output, (2) when not privileged, nsight may not attach to processes launched by the container runtime => missing kernels. For (1) set `--userns=keep-id` or pre-create the output dir on the host and chown to the container UID, or set umask inside container.

jordan: alternative for (1): run `nsys` with `--output /traces/run1` but mount `/traces` from host and `chown 1000:1000 /traces` in init step. For (2) if you can't run privileged in staging, use `nsys profile --capture-range=cudaProfilerApi` and instrument the app to start/stop captures (less intrusive).

maria: another gotcha — when we profile with small batches the runtime fires many tiny kernels (KV cache lookups + attention fragments) which look like a perf regression. follow-up is to compare kernel timelines between a baseline run and the suspect run and check kernel durations distribution rather than total number. I attached a quick grep to show the pattern: `grep -E "(gemm|attention|kvcache)" run1.qdrep | wc -l` (we saw 5k launches vs 300 in baseline).

alex: nice call. our telemetry shows an uptick in "kernel churn" around the time we changed batching heuristics last deploy. could be that the batching sharding is splitting sequences too aggressively and eliminating multi-row GEMMs.

jordan: yep, when batch heuristic sets `max_tokens_per_batch` too low you get more kernel-shape changes and worse kernel selection by the compiler (fallbacks). try bumping `batch_max_tokens` to 128/256 and re-profile. also check that quantization path isn't forcing a slow fallback kernel like `cublas_gemm_ex_fallback`.

alex: ran an isolated experiment with `batch_max_tokens=256` and the timeline looks better — fewer, longer GEMM kernels. but still missing some kernels in the non-priv run.

sara: for the missing kernels in non-priv runs, try the host attach workflow: run the container with `--pid=host` and then do a host-side `nsys attach --pid <container_pid> --output /host_traces/run1`. That avoids container-level restrictions but needs host access.

maria: if host attach is not possible, perfetto aperiodic tracing helped us capture kernel timings without requiring CAP_SYS_ADMIN. it's lower fidelity for CUDA driver internals but often enough to detect hotspot shifts.

alex: low-effort checklist I'm going to run this afternoon:
- repro in a privileged staging pod (quick)
- reproduce root-owned .qdrep by creating traces from init container to see chown race
- rerun with batch_max_tokens 128/256 to confirm kernel churn hypothesis
- produce side-by-side flame charts for baseline vs suspect

jordan: ping me when you have the privileged trace; I can run kernel-selection diffs and look for fallback kernels. also if you can attach the .qdrep (or export CSV of kernel events) I'll script a quick aggregation for GEMM/attention latencies.

alex: will do, thanks. tagging this as follow-up for perf infra: https://redwood-internal/boards/infra/issue/1117 (note: needs a permission flow so engineers can collect traces from staging without full privileges). :thumbsup:

sara: one last note — if you keep hitting ownership races, add `--security-opt label=disable` to the pod (openshift quirk) or make the traces dir a persistent volume with proper fsGroup in the pod spec.

maria: great thread. small reminder: when you upload .qdrep to the perf bucket, include the container image digest and the exact batching config so we can correlate.

alex: thanks all — I'll post results in this thread after the privileged run completes.
